articles.title: NetDocuments CPO Dan Hauck On The Company’s Redesigned Platform, The Legal Context Graph, And Building An Agentic DMS
articles.content:
As NetDocuments rolls out a completely redesigned user experience, a new Microsoft 365 integration, and real-time co-authoring, LawNext host Bob Ambrogi speaks with Chief Product Officer Dan Hauck in an episode recorded live at the company’s Inspire conference in Orlando in October. Hauck, who last appeared on the show in 2022, explains how the company rethought its interface for an agent-ready world, why customers can switch freely between the old and new experiences with no forced migration, and how the new M365 add-in replaces legacy desktop integrations so lawyers can work across Windows, Mac and mobile devices.
(This is the second of three episodes we recorded at Inspire. Last week, we posted Bob’s interview with Josh Baxter, CEO of NetDocuments.)
Hauck also digs into the legal context graph, the proprietary knowledge infrastructure the company launched earlier this year that continuously maps the relationships among every matter, document, communication and person across a firm’s entire document repository. He explains how it works, how it helps agents perform better, and how it can dramatically reduce the cost of token consumption. He also walks through other NetDocuments’ announcements, including the general availability of tabular review, new document generation and redlining in the NetDocuments assistant, interactive HTML reports, and a beta MCP connector with Legora that joins existing connectors to Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, and others.
A former litigator who founded ThreadKM before NetDocuments acquired it, Hauck draws parallels between today’s AI shift and the early days of technology-assisted review in e-discovery, when lawyers first learned to pair human judgment with machine speed. He discusses why NetDocuments keeps investing in its own interface even as MCP lets users reach their documents from other AI platforms, how smaller and midsized firms can benefit from the context graph without dedicated knowledge management staff, and what an agentic DMS might look like in daily practice.

articles.title: It All Hinges On Judgment. And Human Connections.
articles.content:
Right before ClioCon and the release of Clio’s Legal Trends Report, an interesting article appeared. Both the Clio Report and an earlier one from 8am showed billable hours going up, even though AI was supposed to bring them down, a paradox which Joe Patrice discussed in a recent article. The article I’m referring to suggests we aren’t seeing, and may never see, the across the board efficiency gains from AI so many predict. Why? Because we’re humans. Gulp.
The article was by Torsten Slok, the chief economist and a partner at Apollo Global Management, a major alternative investment manager. Prior to Apollo, he worked for 15 years at Deutsche Bank. Before that, he was with the International Monetary Fund and the OECD.
So he’s no dummy. But he is known for challenging conventional wisdom. My kind of guy, since over the years I’ve too often found that so-called “conventional wisdom” is, well, just conventional folly.
Slok’s Swimming Against The Stream
Slok’s recent article certainly challenges what most people are thinking these days. He bluntly argues, “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech.”
Whoa. Zero? That can’t be, right? I mean, AI is supposed to have disrupted work and just about every business. But Slok says the data show that revenue per employee and profit margins have remained largely flat among S&P 500 companies outside the Magnificent Seven (think Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, etc.). And importantly, says Slok, “there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth.”
What does that mean? “With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.” (Tokens being the meter that runs every time you use an AI tool. I know, these guys can never use a term that we all understand.) That, in turn, means that mainstream corporate America may soon decide it doesn’t need the new shiny AI toys. And won’t be willing to pay for them.
But That’s Not All
But that’s not all, says Slok. He speculates that turning AI into revenue growth and higher profit margins may not be as easy as everyone thinks:
AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment. Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.
Emphasis in original.
Hmm. Judgment. Context. Ethics. Sounds like things most agree lawyers provide.
AI and Legal
Which is why Slok’s ideas are particularly chilling when it comes to AI hype in legal. Certainly, AI can boost profits in most any law firm by automating back-office tasks. But that mostly cuts costs. It affects revenue only indirectly, by giving the revenue producers more time to bill hours. Which may explain what Clio and 8am are seeing. But beyond that, you run square into a paradox. Every billable hour AI saves is an hour of lost revenue. There is no getting around it.
And as the cost of AI tokens goes up along with the price of those fancy AI tools, law firm management may ask a legitimate question. Why should we be buying stuff that’s just going to reduce our profits?
So unlike corporate America, where AI could conceivably increase revenue per worker and profit margins (even if it hasn’t yet), given the predominant law firm business model, it may never do so.
Of course, that’s not the end of the story. You still have those law firm customers: the clients. Clients who could start demanding to see AI use reflected in their bills. Or they will vote with their feet and go to firms where they do see it. Or do more in-house.
Law Runs on Judgment
But that’s where the other part of Slok’s hypothesis comes into play. Perhaps even more so than in any other business, judgment is critical to the successful handling of most legal problems. And things like context, trust, culture, and ethics go hand in hand with the exercise of that judgment.
It’s the ability to predict what your client will want, even before they know it. It’s the ability to predict what your adversary will do. (There’s nothing like telling your client at what point the other side will seek settlement. And being right.) It’s knowing the difference between a fair and achievable result and one that will never happen. It’s the basic understanding of ethics.
Judgment Translates Into Value
So even if AI can reduce hours (and there’s some question about that; stay tuned for more in my next article), the price of that judgment could go up. Way up. Judgment becomes more valuable when everyone else is thinking with AI. And as its price goes up, the savings from AI go down.
Moreover, since so much of law hinges on judgment, judgment that AI can’t provide, even widespread AI use would do little to reduce the value and overall cost of legal services. And if AI doesn’t reduce the client’s cost, the client has little reason to demand it. Or for law firms to buy those shiny new toys.
In addition, even if legal America ever figures out how to make alternative fees work effectively, there will still be a premium on that judgment built into the fee.
It’s Still All About Us Humans
As the Clio study shows, the simple fact is that AI has not yet produced the same kind of savings on the substantive side that it has on the back-office side. And if people like Slok are right, then adoption of AI on the substantive side may be slow going. And that wholesale reduction in fees may never happen, at least in the ways we think.
All of which is to say that it may not yet be time to accept all the conventional wisdom and AI gushing that’s going on. AI may transform legal, but it probably won’t do it in ways that can be and are being predicted. Unless it somehow replaces judgment and a human’s ability to understand another human. Which is what practicing law is all about.
In a world of conventional wisdom, it’s nice to have someone like Slok track mud all over the carpet.
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.

articles.title: Make 2027 The Year You Start Your Law Practice
articles.content:
Free Webinar | Friday, November 20, 2026 | 3:00 PM ET
Thinking about starting your own law firm? With AI transforming the legal profession and changing the economics of running a practice, 2027 might be the perfect time to make that move.
On Friday, November 20, at 3 PM ET, I’m hosting a free webinar, Make 2027 the Year You Start Your Law Practice, where I’ll share what I’ve learned from more than three decades of running my own firm, what I’d do differently if I were starting today, and why I believe there are exciting opportunities ahead for lawyers ready to go out on their own.
I’m also considering an optional, hands-on workshop on December 12 in the DC/VA/MD area for those who want to take the next step and actually begin setting up their firms.
You’ll find all the details, including information about the proposed workshop, on the registration page.
Stop loaning your talent. Start owning your future.
Make 2027 the year you start your law practice.
